name: Quit smoking / vaping

lead: Quitting tobacco or vaping is cited as a way to avoid or reduce 'smoker's face', the pattern of wrinkles, sagging and a dull yellowish or grayish complexion seen in many long-term smokers.

Medical sources attribute these changes to reduced oxygen and nutrient supply to skin, narrowed blood vessels, oxidative stress and breakdown of collagen and elastin. The link between smoking and facial aging is documented in observational research. No trials of quitting for appearance were found, and vaping and facial aging have not been studied.

paras: People quit through whatever route works for them, including nicotine replacement, medication or support programmes, and often mention it as part of a broader skin and anti-aging routine. Skin blood flow is the step through which any appearance change is expected.
Quitting itself carries no appearance-specific risks in the sources reviewed. Smoking is linked to many serious diseases, so quitting has health benefits well beyond looks.

web.title: What happens to your skin when you quit smoking - Healthline

chain: Better skin blood flow and collagen
angle.text: Quitting tobacco or vaping is cited to avoid or reduce smoker's face, with its wrinkles, sagging and dull yellowish complexion. Less tobacco and nicotine exposure means better skin blood flow and collagen, and a brighter, less wrinkled complexion. The link between smoking and facial aging comes from observational research.

lead: Quitting smoking or vaping is discussed in skincare and looksmaxxing circles as a way to protect and improve the skin. Long-term smokers often show a recognisable set of facial changes called 'smoker's face': wrinkling, sagging, a greyish or yellowish complexion and staining of the teeth and mouth [1]. Stopping tobacco is the step people take to stop adding to that pattern, and some report a clearer, more even complexion afterwards.

The skin-related reasons given include better oxygen and nutrient supply to the skin, less breakdown of collagen and elastin, and less oxidative stress [1]. A 1985 BMJ study cited by Wikipedia found the characteristic features in about 46% of continuing smokers but only about 8% of former smokers with a similar smoking history [1]. A health-information article summarising several small studies reports less redness, tobacco staining and discolouration after quitting, and renewed collagen production in a small 2019 study [2].

Vaping is a separate topic. E-cigarettes avoid combustion, and a 2025 Cochrane review cited on Wikipedia found nicotine e-cigarettes more effective than nicotine replacement therapy for quitting smoking [3]. Researchers studying vaping have mostly looked at lung and cardiovascular effects rather than the skin [4][5]. On looksmax.org some users describe nicotine as an appetite suppressant for getting lean, while others say they quit because of concerns about growth and health [6][7][8].
infobox: Even skin tone, fewer wrinkles, cleaner teeth, healthier complexion
Nicotine replacement, varenicline, vaping cessation programs
Skin colour changes begin to reverse within weeks, per small studies [2]

paras: Smoker's face refers to the facial changes seen in many long-term tobacco smokers, including wrinkling, sagging, a grey tone to the skin, hair loss and mouth changes such as staining, gum disease and bad breath [1]. Quitting removes the ongoing exposure behind these features.

Health-information summaries describe improvements after quitting: age spots and discolouration beginning to fade within about a month in one review, skin colour changes starting to reverse four to twelve weeks after stopping in a small 2013 study, and a small 2010 study estimating a 'biological age' reduction of 13 years based on brightness, smoothness and elasticity [2]. The same summary notes that more research is needed on how quitting affects existing wrinkles and that timing varies between people [2].

Proposed mechanisms include higher levels of enzymes that break down collagen, elastin and proteoglycans, lower antioxidant levels such as vitamin C, narrowing of facial blood vessels by tobacco chemicals, and a build-up of free radicals causing oxidative stress [1]. Quitting is described as allowing collagen production to resume, based on a small 2019 study [2].

Wikipedia lists staining or yellowing of teeth, gum disease, tooth loss and halitosis among smoker's face features, and reduced odour and fewer stains are among the reasons users give for choosing e-cigarettes over cigarettes [1][3].

E-liquids typically contain propylene glycol, glycerin, flavourings and often nicotine, and heating them produces by-products including formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and acrolein [3]. Wikipedia describes vaping as less harmful than smoking but not free of risk [3].

Research on vaping has concentrated on lung injury, including the 2019 EVALI outbreak, and on cardiovascular effects [4][5][9]. An American Heart Association scientific statement discusses patterns of use and potential harms [10]. Studies of vaping with facial appearance as the outcome were not located.

Randomised trials have tested programs for quitting vaping, including a text-message program for young adults, a text-message program for adolescents and a varenicline trial in youth [11][12][13]. Their outcomes concern quitting rates, not appearance.

Posts on looksmax.org about nicotine are mixed. Some users describe vaping as an appetite suppressant that helped them lose weight and show a leaner face, while other users reply with concerns about lungs and about growth in younger users [6][7][8]. Other threads describe the difficulty of the first days without nicotine [14].

No randomised trial of quitting smoking or vaping with facial appearance as the primary outcome was found. The skin findings come from observational and small studies summarised above [1][2]. Randomised trials of cessation programs measure whether people stop using nicotine [11][12][13].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, vaping and nicotine come up both as a way to suppress appetite and get lean and as something users say they are trying to give up.
